title: Absolute vs relative uncertainty
definition: Absolute uncertainty is the plus-or-minus margin attached to a measurement in the SAME units as the measurement itself (e.g. ±0.1 cm) — it tells you the size of the wobble on this one number. Relative uncertainty instead expresses that same margin as a fraction (or percentage) of the measured value, which is what lets you compare how "good" two completely different measurements are even though they're in different units and different sizes. A ±0.1 cm uncertainty is excellent for a 24.6 cm length but would be terrible for a 0.2 cm one — the absolute number alone can't tell you that, only the relative (percentage) version can.
whenToUse: Use relative uncertainty whenever you need to compare the QUALITY of two different measurements, or whenever a formula (like the multiplication/division propagation rule) asks for uncertainty as a fraction rather than an absolute margin.
formula: relative uncertainty = (absolute uncertainty) / (measured value)

formulaBreakdown.meaning: the ± margin in the same units as the measurement (e.g. ±0.1 cm).
the reading itself that the uncertainty is attached to.
a unit-less fraction (multiply by 100 for a percentage) — lets you compare precision across different instruments and quantities.

code:
import csv
import io

csv_text = """quantity,value,uncertainty
length_cm,24.6,0.1
mass_g,182.4,0.5"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))

for r in rows:
    value = float(r["value"])
    abs_u = float(r["uncertainty"])
    rel_u = abs_u / value
    rel_pct = rel_u * 100
    print(f"{r['quantity']}: value = {value}, absolute uncertainty = {abs_u}")
    print(f"  relative uncertainty = {abs_u} / {value} = {rel_u:.4f} = {rel_pct:.2f}%")
datasetNote: Two independent measurements (a length and a mass) each with their own absolute uncertainty.
output:
length_cm: value = 24.6, absolute uncertainty = 0.1
  relative uncertainty = 0.1 / 24.6 = 0.0041 = 0.41%
mass_g: value = 182.4, absolute uncertainty = 0.5
  relative uncertainty = 0.5 / 182.4 = 0.0027 = 0.27%
caveat: A small absolute uncertainty can still be a LARGE relative uncertainty on a small measurement — always check the relative number before deciding a measurement is "precise enough."

title: Reading uncertainty off an instrument
definition: Every analog instrument (a ruler, a graduated cylinder, an analog thermometer) has a smallest marked division — the finest gradation printed on its scale. Because a human eye can reliably judge whether a reading falls closer to one mark or the next but can't split that gap infinitely finely, the standard convention is to report the reading's uncertainty as half of that smallest division, not the whole division and not zero. This isn't a guess: it reflects the real limit of how finely a human (or the instrument's construction) can resolve a position between two marks.
whenToUse: Use this the moment you take ANY single reading off an analog scale, before you've even done any calculation — it's the starting uncertainty that then propagates through every formula that uses that reading.
formula: reading uncertainty = (smallest division) / 2

formulaBreakdown.meaning: the finest gradation marked on the instrument's scale (e.g. 1 mm marks on a ruler).
halving reflects that a careful reader can judge “about halfway between marks” reliably, but not finer than that.

code:
import csv
import io

# A ruler marked in mm (smallest division = 1 mm). Reading uncertainty is
# taken as half the smallest division.
csv_text = """instrument,smallest_division_mm,reading_mm
ruler,1.0,146.0"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
r = rows[0]
smallest_div = float(r["smallest_division_mm"])
reading = float(r["reading_mm"])
half_div = smallest_div / 2

print(f"smallest division = {smallest_div} mm")
print(f"reading uncertainty = half the smallest division = {smallest_div} / 2 = {half_div} mm")
print(f"reported length = {reading} +/- {half_div} mm")
datasetNote: A ruler marked in 1 mm divisions used to measure a 146.0 mm length.
output:
smallest division = 1.0 mm
reading uncertainty = half the smallest division = 1.0 / 2 = 0.5 mm
reported length = 146.0 +/- 0.5 mm
caveat: This rule is for READING uncertainty only — it doesn't include other error sources like the ruler being warped or held at an angle (parallax), which need their own separate uncertainty terms.

title: Combining repeated readings (mean ± SEM)
definition: When you measure the SAME thing several times, the individual readings scatter around a true value due to random measurement noise. Averaging them (the mean) cancels out much of that noise, and the standard error of the mean (SEM = SD/√n) is the uncertainty on THAT average — it answers "how far off might my reported mean be from the true value," which is a different question from "how spread out were my individual readings" (that's what the SD answers). Because SEM shrinks as n grows, taking more repeated readings is the most direct way to reduce your reported uncertainty.
whenToUse: Use mean ± SEM as your reported result whenever you've taken multiple independent readings of the exact same quantity and want the single best estimate plus its uncertainty.
formula: x̄ ± SEM,  where SEM = s / √n

formulaBreakdown.meaning: the mean of your repeated readings — the best single estimate of the true value.
the sample standard deviation of the individual readings (how spread out THEY are, not how uncertain the mean is).
the square root of how many readings you took — dividing by it is why more repeats shrink the uncertainty.

code:
import csv
import io
import numpy as np

csv_text = """trial,mass_g
1,12.4
2,12.6
3,12.3
4,12.7
5,12.5"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
masses = [float(r["mass_g"]) for r in rows]

n = len(masses)
mean = sum(masses) / n
print(f"readings = {masses}")
print(f"n = {n}")
print(f"mean = {mean:.3f} g")

sq_devs = [(x - mean) ** 2 for x in masses]
variance = sum(sq_devs) / (n - 1)
sd = variance ** 0.5
print(f"sample SD = sqrt(sum((x-mean)^2)/(n-1)) = {sd:.4f} g")

sem = sd / (n ** 0.5)
print(f"SEM = SD / sqrt(n) = {sd:.4f} / sqrt({n}) = {sem:.4f} g")
print(f"reported result = {mean:.2f} +/- {sem:.2f} g")

print(f"check: np.std(masses, ddof=1)/sqrt(n) = {np.std(masses, ddof=1)/np.sqrt(n):.4f} g")
datasetNote: Five repeated mass readings of the same object on the same balance.
output:
readings = [12.4, 12.6, 12.3, 12.7, 12.5]
n = 5
mean = 12.500 g
sample SD = sqrt(sum((x-mean)^2)/(n-1)) = 0.1581 g
SEM = SD / sqrt(n) = 0.1581 / sqrt(5) = 0.0707 g
reported result = 12.50 +/- 0.07 g
check: np.std(masses, ddof=1)/sqrt(n) = 0.0707 g
caveat: SEM measures how well you know the MEAN, not how consistent any single reading is — don't quote the SEM as if it described the spread of an individual future measurement; that's what the SD is for.

title: Uncertainty propagation — addition/subtraction
definition: When you add or subtract two measured quantities, the uncertainties don't cancel or subtract even if the values do — they ADD, because each measurement's error could independently push the result in the worse direction. Subtracting two lengths to get a difference removes none of the measurement wobble in either one; if anything, a small difference between two large, uncertain numbers can end up with an uncertainty that's a LARGE fraction of the result. This is the single most common propagation mistake: assuming subtraction "cancels" the error the way it cancels the value.
whenToUse: Use this whenever your final quantity is a SUM or DIFFERENCE of two or more independently measured values (e.g. a height computed as a total stack height minus a base height).
formula: δ(A ± B) = δA + δB

formulaBreakdown.meaning: the two measured quantities being added or subtracted.
each quantity's own absolute uncertainty.
the propagated absolute uncertainty on the sum OR the difference — the rule is identical either way.

code:
import csv
import io

# Two lengths measured with a ruler, each +/- 0.1 cm, combined by subtraction
# (final height = total stack height - base height).
csv_text = """segment,length_cm,uncertainty_cm
stack_total,18.4,0.1
base,6.2,0.1"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
total = float(rows[0]["length_cm"])
u_total = float(rows[0]["uncertainty_cm"])
base = float(rows[1]["length_cm"])
u_base = float(rows[1]["uncertainty_cm"])

diff = total - base
u_diff = u_total + u_base

print(f"total = {total} +/- {u_total} cm")
print(f"base = {base} +/- {u_base} cm")
print(f"difference = {total} - {base} = {diff:.1f} cm")
print(f"uncertainty adds (even for subtraction!): {u_total} + {u_base} = {u_diff:.1f} cm")
print(f"reported result = {diff:.1f} +/- {u_diff:.1f} cm")
datasetNote: A total stack height and a base height, each measured with the same ruler (±0.1 cm reading uncertainty).
output:
total = 18.4 +/- 0.1 cm
base = 6.2 +/- 0.1 cm
difference = 18.4 - 6.2 = 12.2 cm
uncertainty adds (even for subtraction!): 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.2 cm
reported result = 12.2 +/- 0.2 cm
caveat: Subtracting two nearly-equal large numbers can make the RELATIVE uncertainty on the difference huge even when each input looked precise — always re-check the relative uncertainty on a subtracted result before trusting it.

title: Uncertainty propagation — multiplication/division
definition: When you multiply or divide two measured quantities (like computing a density from mass and volume), you can't just add the absolute uncertainties the way you would for a sum — the units don't match (grams vs cubic centimeters). Instead you convert each measurement's uncertainty to a RELATIVE (fractional) uncertainty first, add those unit-less fractions together, and then convert back to an absolute uncertainty on the final computed result. This is exactly why "absolute vs relative uncertainty" is worth understanding on its own before this rule makes sense.
whenToUse: Use this whenever your final quantity is a PRODUCT or RATIO of two or more independently measured values (density, speed, concentration, rate constants, etc.).
formula: δ(A·B)/(A·B) = δA/A + δB/B

formulaBreakdown.meaning: each input's relative uncertainty (its absolute uncertainty divided by its own value).
the propagated RELATIVE uncertainty of the product (or ratio) — the fractions add, not the raw numbers.
multiply the propagated relative uncertainty by the computed result itself to get an absolute uncertainty in the result's own units.

code:
import csv
import io

# Density = mass / volume, each measured with its own absolute uncertainty.
csv_text = """quantity,value,uncertainty
mass_g,45.2,0.2
volume_cm3,12.0,0.3"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
mass = float(rows[0]["value"])
u_mass = float(rows[0]["uncertainty"])
vol = float(rows[1]["value"])
u_vol = float(rows[1]["uncertainty"])

density = mass / vol
rel_mass = u_mass / mass
rel_vol = u_vol / vol
rel_density = rel_mass + rel_vol
u_density = rel_density * density

print(f"mass = {mass} +/- {u_mass} g -> relative uncertainty = {u_mass}/{mass} = {rel_mass:.4f}")
print(f"volume = {vol} +/- {u_vol} cm^3 -> relative uncertainty = {u_vol}/{vol} = {rel_vol:.4f}")
print(f"density = mass/volume = {mass}/{vol} = {density:.4f} g/cm^3")
print(f"relative uncertainty adds: {rel_mass:.4f} + {rel_vol:.4f} = {rel_density:.4f}")
print(f"absolute uncertainty = {rel_density:.4f} * {density:.4f} = {u_density:.4f} g/cm^3")
print(f"reported result = {density:.2f} +/- {u_density:.2f} g/cm^3")
datasetNote: A mass and a volume measurement, each with its own absolute uncertainty, combined into a density.
output:
mass = 45.2 +/- 0.2 g -> relative uncertainty = 0.2/45.2 = 0.0044
volume = 12.0 +/- 0.3 cm^3 -> relative uncertainty = 0.3/12.0 = 0.0250
density = mass/volume = 45.2/12.0 = 3.7667 g/cm^3
relative uncertainty adds: 0.0044 + 0.0250 = 0.0294
absolute uncertainty = 0.0294 * 3.7667 = 0.1108 g/cm^3
reported result = 3.77 +/- 0.11 g/cm^3
caveat: Don't average the two RELATIVE uncertainties — they add. A common mistake is treating this rule like the addition rule and just adding the absolute uncertainties directly, which is only valid for sums/differences, not products/ratios.

title: Uncertainty propagation — through a power
definition: When a measured quantity is raised to a power (like radius squared in a circle's area formula), its relative uncertainty doesn't just carry through unchanged — it gets MULTIPLIED by the exponent, because a small error in the base gets applied twice (once for each factor) when you square it. This is a special case of the multiplication rule above: x² is really x times itself, so the relative uncertainty adds to itself once for each power, i.e. gets multiplied by the exponent.
whenToUse: Use this whenever a formula raises one of your measured quantities to a power greater than 1 (area from radius, volume from a side length, kinetic energy from velocity, etc.) — a squared radius makes your uncertainty balloon faster than you'd expect.
formula: δ(xⁿ)/xⁿ = n · (δx/x)

formulaBreakdown.meaning: the measured base quantity (e.g. a radius).
the exponent the base is raised to (2 for a squared term, 3 for a cubed term, etc.).
the relative uncertainty in the powered result — n times bigger than the relative uncertainty in x alone.

code:
import csv
import io

# Area of a circle = pi * r^2. Uncertainty in r propagates through the power
# by multiplying the relative uncertainty by the exponent.
csv_text = """quantity,value,uncertainty
radius_cm,5.0,0.2"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
r = float(rows[0]["value"])
u_r = float(rows[0]["uncertainty"])

import math
area = math.pi * r ** 2
rel_r = u_r / r
n = 2  # exponent
rel_area = n * rel_r
u_area = rel_area * area

print(f"radius = {r} +/- {u_r} cm -> relative uncertainty = {u_r}/{r} = {rel_r:.4f}")
print(f"area = pi * r^2 = {area:.4f} cm^2")
print(f"power rule: relative uncertainty in r^{n} = {n} * relative uncertainty in r = {n} * {rel_r:.4f} = {rel_area:.4f}")
print(f"absolute uncertainty = {rel_area:.4f} * {area:.4f} = {u_area:.4f} cm^2")
print(f"reported result = {area:.2f} +/- {u_area:.2f} cm^2")
datasetNote: A single radius measurement with its absolute uncertainty, used to compute a circle's area (which depends on r²).
output:
radius = 5.0 +/- 0.2 cm -> relative uncertainty = 0.2/5.0 = 0.0400
area = pi * r^2 = 78.5398 cm^2
power rule: relative uncertainty in r^2 = 2 * relative uncertainty in r = 2 * 0.0400 = 0.0800
absolute uncertainty = 0.0800 * 78.5398 = 6.2832 cm^2
reported result = 78.54 +/- 6.28 cm^2
caveat: A modest 4% uncertainty in a radius becomes an 8% uncertainty in the AREA because of the squared exponent — always check whether your formula squares or cubes an input before assuming uncertainty carries through unchanged.

title: Type A vs Type B uncertainty
definition: Type A uncertainty comes from STATISTICS — you took repeated readings and computed a spread (like the SEM) from the scatter you actually observed. Type B uncertainty comes from EVERYTHING ELSE you know about the measurement that repetition alone can't reveal — a manufacturer's stated instrument tolerance, a calibration certificate, or a known rounding limit — estimated by judgement or a spec sheet rather than by repeating the measurement. A single reported result usually needs BOTH combined, because repeating a reading on a slightly-miscalibrated meter ten times will make Type A look small while the meter is still systematically off — that's exactly what Type B catches.
whenToUse: Use Type A when you have multiple repeated readings to compute a spread from; use Type B whenever an instrument's own documented tolerance/spec is a real source of error that repeating the reading would never reveal, then combine both (added in quadrature) into one final uncertainty.
formula: u_combined = √( u_A² + u_B² )

formulaBreakdown.meaning: Type A uncertainty — estimated statistically from the observed scatter in repeated readings (e.g. the SEM).
Type B uncertainty — estimated from other information, like a manufacturer's spec sheet, not from repetition.
the two independent uncertainty sources combine as √(sum of squares), not a simple sum — the same logic as a right-triangle hypotenuse.

code:
import csv
import io

# Type A: from repeated readings (statistical, SEM). Type B: from a fixed
# instrument spec (e.g. manufacturer-stated tolerance), not from repetition.
csv_text = """trial,voltage_v
1,4.98
2,5.01
3,4.99
4,5.02
5,5.00"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
voltages = [float(r["voltage_v"]) for r in rows]
n = len(voltages)
mean = sum(voltages) / n
variance = sum((v - mean) ** 2 for v in voltages) / (n - 1)
sd = variance ** 0.5
sem = sd / (n ** 0.5)

print(f"readings = {voltages}")
print(f"Type A (statistical, from repetition): mean = {mean:.3f} V, SEM = {sem:.4f} V")

meter_spec_pct = 0.005  # manufacturer states +/- 0.5% of reading
type_b = mean * meter_spec_pct
print(f"Type B (from the multimeter's spec sheet, +/-0.5% of reading, NOT from repeating trials):")
print(f"  {mean:.3f} * {meter_spec_pct} = {type_b:.4f} V")

combined = (sem ** 2 + type_b ** 2) ** 0.5
print(f"combined uncertainty (add in quadrature) = sqrt({sem:.4f}^2 + {type_b:.4f}^2) = {combined:.4f} V")
print(f"reported result = {mean:.3f} +/- {combined:.3f} V")
datasetNote: Five repeated voltage readings on a multimeter that also carries a manufacturer-stated ±0.5%-of-reading spec.
output:
readings = [4.98, 5.01, 4.99, 5.02, 5.0]
Type A (statistical, from repetition): mean = 5.000 V, SEM = 0.0071 V
Type B (from the multimeter's spec sheet, +/-0.5% of reading, NOT from repeating trials):
  5.000 * 0.005 = 0.0250 V
combined uncertainty (add in quadrature) = sqrt(0.0071^2 + 0.0250^2) = 0.0260 V
reported result = 5.000 +/- 0.026 V
caveat: Repeating a reading many times shrinks the Type A term but does NOTHING to shrink Type B — you cannot statistics your way out of a miscalibrated or under-specified instrument.

title: Rounding the uncertainty to 1–2 sig figs
definition: An uncertainty computed from a formula (like SD/√n) often comes out with many meaningless decimal digits — the convention is to round the UNCERTAINTY itself to just 1 or 2 significant figures first, since knowing your error margin to 5 decimal places is never meaningful. Then, and only then, you round the measured VALUE to match the same last decimal place as the (already-rounded) uncertainty — not the other way around. Doing it in this order avoids the common mistake of reporting a value to more decimal places than the uncertainty could possibly justify.
whenToUse: Use this as the final formatting step for EVERY reported value ± uncertainty pair, right before writing up a result — it's what turns a raw computed number into a properly reported scientific result.
formula: round(uncertainty) first → then round(value) to the SAME decimal place

formulaBreakdown.meaning: to 1–2 significant figures — e.g. a raw SEM of 0.012909... becomes 0.01.
round the measured value to the SAME last decimal place the rounded uncertainty landed on, not to its own “natural” precision.

code:
import csv
import io

# Reporting convention: value +/- uncertainty (unit), uncertainty rounded to
# 1-2 sig figs, value's last decimal place matched to it.
csv_text = """trial,length_cm
1,9.83
2,9.79
3,9.85
4,9.81"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
lengths = [float(r["length_cm"]) for r in rows]
n = len(lengths)
mean = sum(lengths) / n
variance = sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in lengths) / (n - 1)
sd = variance ** 0.5
sem_raw = sd / (n ** 0.5)

print(f"readings = {lengths}")
print(f"raw mean = {mean}")
print(f"raw SEM = {sem_raw}")

# Round uncertainty to 1 sig fig first
sem_rounded = round(sem_raw, 2)
print(f"round SEM to 1-2 sig figs -> {sem_rounded} cm")

mean_rounded = round(mean, 2)
print(f"match the value's last decimal place to the uncertainty's -> mean = {mean_rounded} cm")
print(f"reported result: length = {mean_rounded} +/- {sem_rounded} cm")
datasetNote: Four repeated length readings, whose raw mean and SEM both come out with many decimal digits before rounding.
output:
readings = [9.83, 9.79, 9.85, 9.81]
raw mean = 9.82
raw SEM = 0.012909944487358126
round SEM to 1-2 sig figs -> 0.01 cm
match the value's last decimal place to the uncertainty's -> mean = 9.82 cm
reported result: length = 9.82 +/- 0.01 cm
caveat: Reporting "9.821 ± 0.012909944 cm" is wrong even though it's mathematically what the calculator spat out — an uncertainty is never known to 8 significant figures, so trailing digits past the 1–2 sig-fig cutoff are meaningless noise, not extra precision.

title: Calibration against a known reference
definition: Calibration means checking an instrument's reading against a quantity whose TRUE value is already known (a reference standard, a certified weight, a boiling-point check) before trusting its readings on your actual samples. If the instrument consistently reads high or low on the known standard, that's a systematic offset (bias) — not random noise — and it will bias every future reading on that same instrument in the same direction until it's corrected or the instrument is re-zeroed. Calibration is a Type B uncertainty check: repeating a reading on an uncalibrated scale ten times will never reveal this problem, because every one of those ten readings is wrong in the exact same direction.
whenToUse: Use this before trusting a scale, sensor, or meter for real measurements — especially before a science-fair experiment where the SAME instrument will be reused across every trial, so any bias would otherwise contaminate every single data point identically.
formula: offset = (mean reading of the known standard) − (true reference value)

formulaBreakdown.meaning: a reference object/solution whose true value is already established (e.g. a certified 100.0 g calibration mass).
what the instrument reports when measuring that same known standard, averaged over a few checks.
the systematic bias — subtract this offset from every later reading on that same instrument to correct for it.

code:
import csv
import io

# Calibration: checking an instrument against a KNOWN reference value before
# trusting its readings, and applying a correction offset if it's biased.
csv_text = """reference_standard_g,scale_reading_g
100.0,101.2
100.0,101.3
100.0,101.1"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
readings = [float(r["scale_reading_g"]) for r in rows]
reference = float(rows[0]["reference_standard_g"])

n = len(readings)
mean_reading = sum(readings) / n
print(f"known reference standard mass = {reference} g")
print(f"scale readings of that SAME standard = {readings}")
print(f"mean reading = {mean_reading:.3f} g")

offset = mean_reading - reference
print(f"calibration offset = mean reading - true reference = {mean_reading:.3f} - {reference} = {offset:+.3f} g")
print(f"the scale reads {abs(offset):.3f} g {'high' if offset > 0 else 'low'} on a known {reference} g mass")

# Apply the correction to a real sample measurement taken on the same scale.
sample_reading = 54.6
corrected = sample_reading - offset
print(f"a later sample reads {sample_reading} g on this SAME uncalibrated scale")
print(f"corrected value = {sample_reading} - ({offset:+.3f}) = {corrected:.3f} g")
datasetNote: A balance's readings of a known, certified 100.0 g calibration mass, repeated three times.
output:
known reference standard mass = 100.0 g
scale readings of that SAME standard = [101.2, 101.3, 101.1]
mean reading = 101.200 g
calibration offset = mean reading - true reference = 101.200 - 100.0 = +1.200 g
the scale reads 1.200 g high on a known 100.0 g mass
a later sample reads 54.6 g on this SAME uncalibrated scale
corrected value = 54.6 - (+1.200) = 53.400 g
caveat: A calibration offset only corrects a CONSISTENT bias — if the offset itself drifts over time (e.g. a battery-powered sensor degrading) you need to recalibrate periodically, not just apply one correction forever.

title: Missing (blank) vs zero vs “not measured”
definition: A blank cell (nothing was recorded), a genuine 0 (you measured and the value really was zero), and a sentinel code like -999 or "NM" someone typed to mean "didn't measure this one" are three completely different things that must NEVER be collapsed into each other. Treating a blank as a zero silently drags your mean toward zero for a value that was never actually observed; treating a sentinel code like -999 as a real number is even worse, because it isn't just missing — it actively poisons any arithmetic that includes it. The fix is to explicitly detect and exclude both blanks and sentinel codes BEFORE computing anything, while keeping every genuine, deliberately-recorded 0.
whenToUse: Use this the moment you import any raw dataset, before computing a single mean or SD — scan every column for blanks and any sentinel codes and handle each category explicitly and separately.
formula: clean(x) = exclude if blank OR x == sentinel;  else keep x  (including a genuine 0)

formulaBreakdown.meaning: a cell where nothing at all was entered — truly not measured, must be excluded, never treated as 0.
a placeholder number/code (like -999) someone used to MEAN “not measured” — must be recognized and excluded, not computed with as if it were real.
an actual, deliberately recorded measurement of zero — this must be KEPT, not confused with the other two categories.

code:
import csv
import io

# Blank cell (truly not recorded) vs an explicit 0 (a real measured zero) vs a
# code like -999/"NM" someone used for "not measured" -- these must NOT be
# treated the same way when computing a mean.
csv_text = """plant,leaves_grown
1,4
2,0
3,
4,-999
5,3"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
print("raw rows:")
for r in rows:
    print(f"  plant {r['plant']}: leaves_grown = {r['leaves_grown']!r}")

# Naive (wrong) approach: blindly convert everything to float, treating blank
# as error and -999 as a real value.
cleaned = []
dropped_blank = 0
flagged_sentinel = 0
for r in rows:
    raw = r["leaves_grown"]
    if raw == "":
        dropped_blank += 1
        continue  # truly missing -- not measured, must be excluded, not zeroed
    val = float(raw)
    if val == -999:
        flagged_sentinel += 1
        continue  # -999 is a "not measured" sentinel code, not a real measurement of -999 leaves
    cleaned.append(val)  # includes the genuine 0 -- that IS a measured value

print(f"blank cells excluded (truly missing): {dropped_blank}")
print(f"sentinel -999 cells excluded (recorded as 'not measured', not a real -999): {flagged_sentinel}")
print(f"cleaned values (genuine 0 kept!) = {cleaned}")
print(f"correct mean = {sum(cleaned)/len(cleaned):.3f} (n={len(cleaned)})")

wrong_include_sentinel = [float(r["leaves_grown"]) for r in rows if r["leaves_grown"] != ""]
print(f"WRONG mean if -999 sentinel were treated as real data = {sum(wrong_include_sentinel)/len(wrong_include_sentinel):.3f}")
datasetNote: Five plants' new-leaf counts, including one blank cell, one sentinel -999 code, and one genuine 0.
output:
raw rows:
  plant 1: leaves_grown = '4'
  plant 2: leaves_grown = '0'
  plant 3: leaves_grown = ''
  plant 4: leaves_grown = '-999'
  plant 5: leaves_grown = '3'
blank cells excluded (truly missing): 1
sentinel -999 cells excluded (recorded as 'not measured', not a real -999): 1

title: Listwise deletion and why it can bias results
definition: Listwise deletion means dropping an ENTIRE row the moment any one of its columns is missing — simple, but only safe if which rows go missing has nothing to do with the outcome you're studying. If missingness is instead related to the result (e.g. sicker or slower-growing subjects are disproportionately the ones that never got measured, because they died, wilted, or were harder to read), deleting those rows doesn't just shrink your sample size — it selectively removes exactly the cases that would have pulled your result in an inconvenient direction, silently biasing the remaining average.
whenToUse: Use complete-case (listwise) deletion only after checking WHY each row is missing — if the missingness pattern correlates with your outcome variable, deletion will bias your result and a more careful missing-data method (or at minimum, disclosure of the pattern) is needed instead.
formula: kept rows = { rows with NO missing values in any required column }

formulaBreakdown.meaning: keep only rows where every required column has a value; drop the rest entirely, not just the missing cell.
WHY certain rows are missing — random malfunction (usually safe to delete) vs correlated with the outcome (usually biases the result if deleted).

import csv

# Listwise deletion: drop any row with a missing value in ANY column. Shows

title: Mean/median imputation and its caveat
definition: Imputation means filling a missing cell with a plausible substitute value — commonly the mean or median of the OTHER, observed values in that same column — rather than dropping the whole row. This keeps your sample size intact and avoids the bias risk of listwise deletion, but it comes with its own cost: the imputed value has ZERO real variability of its own (it's a constant you invented), so the dataset's overall spread (SD) shrinks artificially, making your result look more precise/consistent than the real underlying measurements actually were.
whenToUse: Use mean/median imputation when a small number of values are missing for reasons unrelated to the outcome (e.g. a sensor briefly glitched) and you need to preserve sample size — but always disclose which values were imputed and how, and expect the reported SD to be a slight underestimate of the true spread.
formula: xᵢ (imputed) = mean(observed values)   or   median(observed values)

formulaBreakdown.meaning: every value in the column that WASN'T missing — the mean/median used for imputation comes only from these.
the substitute placed into the missing slot — a best guess, not a real measurement, and it carries no measurement noise of its own.

import csv
import io

csv_text = """trial,mass_g
1,10.2
2,10.5
3,

5,10.4"""

values = [r["mass_g"] for r in rows]

median_obs = sorted_obs[len(sorted_obs) // 2]

print(f"mean of observed = {mean_obs:.3f} g")
print(f"median of observed = {median_obs:.3f} g")

imputed_median = [float(v) if v != "" else median_obs for v in values]

print(f"median-imputed series = {[round(x,3) for x in imputed_median]}")

sd_before = (sum((x - mean_obs) ** 2 for x in observed) / (len(observed) - 1)) ** 0.5
mean_after = sum(imputed_mean) / len(imputed_mean)
sd_after = (sum((x - mean_after) ** 2 for x in imputed_mean) / (len(imputed_mean) - 1)) ** 0.5
print(f"SD before imputation (n={len(observed)}) = {sd_before:.4f} g")
print(f"SD after mean-imputation (n={len(imputed_mean)}) = {sd_after:.4f} g")
print("caveat check: imputing the mean for the missing slot shrank the SD --")

title: Last-observation-carried-forward (LOCF) for time series
definition: For data collected in a TIME SEQUENCE (daily temperature logs, growth measured every day), a gap in the middle is often filled by simply repeating the last value that WAS recorded, forward, until a new reading appears — this is last-observation-carried-forward (LOCF). It's a convenient default because it requires no interpolation math, but it silently assumes nothing changed during the gap, which is often false if the underlying quantity was actively trending (rising, falling, or oscillating) right through the missing days.
whenToUse: Use LOCF only as a rough placeholder for short gaps in a slowly-changing time series, and always flag which points were carried forward rather than actually measured — for anything trending quickly, prefer interpolation or simply reporting the gap as missing.
formula: xₜ (missing) = x_last_observed   (repeated forward until the next real reading)

formulaBreakdown.meaning: the most recent value that was ACTUALLY measured before the gap started.
that same last value is copied into every missing time step until a new real reading breaks the chain.

code:
import csv
import io

# Last-observation-carried-forward for a time series with a gap (e.g. a
# sensor logger missed a reading day).
csv_text = """day,temperature_c
1,21.4
2,21.6
3,
4,
5,22.1"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
print("raw series:")
for r in rows:
    print(f"  day {r['day']}: {r['temperature_c']!r}")

filled = []
last_value = None
fill_log = []
for r in rows:
    raw = r["temperature_c"]
    if raw == "":
        if last_value is None:
            raise ValueError("no prior observation to carry forward")
        filled.append(last_value)
        fill_log.append(f"day {r['day']}: missing -> carry forward last value {last_value}")
    else:
        val = float(raw)
        filled.append(val)
        last_value = val

print("fills applied:")
for line in fill_log:
    print(f"  {line}")

print(f"LOCF-filled series = {filled}")
print("caveat check: LOCF assumes the value stayed flat during the gap -- days")
print("3-4 are both stamped at 21.6 even though day 5 shows the temperature")
print("was already climbing, so LOCF likely UNDERSTATES days 3-4.")

  day 2: '21.6'
  day 3: ''
  day 4: ''
  day 5: '22.1'
fills applied:
  day 3: missing -> carry forward last value 21.6
  day 4: missing -> carry forward last value 21.6

3-4 are both stamped at 21.6 even though day 5 shows the temperature
was already climbing, so LOCF likely UNDERSTATES days 3-4.
caveat: LOCF assumes the value was flat during the entire gap — if the surrounding readings show a clear trend (as here, where day 5 shows it was already climbing), LOCF will systematically understate a rising trend and overstate a falling one during the gap.

title: Deduplicating repeated rows
definition: A row can end up duplicated in a dataset for entirely mundane reasons — a spreadsheet paste that got pasted twice, a form that was re-submitted after a page refresh, or a copy-paste error while combining sheets from different lab members. Because every downstream calculation (mean, SD, a statistical test) treats each row as one independent measurement, an accidental duplicate silently gives that ONE real measurement double the weight it should have, quietly pulling the result toward it.
whenToUse: Use this as a required checkpoint immediately after combining data from multiple sources (different lab members' spreadsheets, multiple export files) — check for rows with an identical trial/sample identifier and remove the extras before any calculation.
formula: deduped = { first occurrence of each unique row-id }

formulaBreakdown.meaning: whatever uniquely identifies one real measurement (a trial number, sample id) — duplicates share the SAME id.
once an id has appeared once, any later row with that same id is a duplicate and gets dropped, not averaged in again.

code:
import csv
import io

# Duplicated rows (e.g. a spreadsheet paste that got copy-pasted twice, or a
# form re-submitted after a page refresh) silently inflate n and skew any
# mean that happens to include the duplicated value repeatedly.
csv_text = """trial,germinated_seeds
1,14
2,18
2,18
3,16
4,15"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
print("raw rows:")
for r in rows:
    print(f"  trial {r['trial']}: {r['germinated_seeds']}")

seen = set()
deduped = []
removed = []
for r in rows:
    key = r["trial"]
    if key in seen:
        removed.append(r)
        continue
    seen.add(key)
    deduped.append(r)

print(f"duplicate trial ids removed: {[r['trial'] for r in removed]}")

raw_values = [float(r["germinated_seeds"]) for r in rows]
deduped_values = [float(r["germinated_seeds"]) for r in deduped]
print(f"mean WITH duplicate = {sum(raw_values)/len(raw_values):.3f} (n={len(raw_values)})")
print(f"mean AFTER dedup = {sum(deduped_values)/len(deduped_values):.3f} (n={len(deduped_values)})")

  trial 2: 18
  trial 2: 18
  trial 3: 16
  trial 4: 15

title: Range/sanity validation for physically impossible values
definition: Many measured quantities have a physically possible range that no real reading can ever fall outside — pH between 0 and 14, a percentage between 0 and 100, an animal's mass that can't be negative. Range validation means checking every value against those hard physical bounds BEFORE any statistics are computed, flagging anything outside them as an entry error, sensor glitch, or transcription mistake — not averaging it in as if it were a real (if unusual) measurement.
whenToUse: Use this as an automatic first-pass check on any numeric column that has a known physical floor and/or ceiling — it catches decimal-point typos (170 instead of 17.0) and sensor faults before they ever reach your mean or SD.
formula: flag x if x < physical_min OR x > physical_max

formulaBreakdown.meaning: the hard, known bounds a real measurement of this quantity can NEVER cross (e.g. pH ∈ [0, 14]).
a value outside the bounds is almost certainly an error, not a real extreme measurement — investigate it rather than quietly including or excluding it.

code:
import csv
import io

# Physically-impossible-value validation: a pH sensor cannot read below 0 or
# above 14; flag anything outside that range as a probable data-entry or
# sensor error rather than silently averaging it in.
csv_text = """sample,ph_reading
1,6.8
2,7.1
3,17.2
4,6.9
5,-0.4"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
LOWER, UPPER = 0.0, 14.0

valid = []
flagged = []
for r in rows:
    val = float(r["ph_reading"])
    if val < LOWER or val > UPPER:
        flagged.append((r["sample"], val))
    else:
        valid.append(val)

print(f"valid range for pH: [{LOWER}, {UPPER}]")
for sample, val in flagged:
    print(f"  sample {sample}: {val} is OUTSIDE the physically possible pH range -- flagged, not averaged in")

print(f"valid readings kept = {valid}")
print(f"mean of valid readings only = {sum(valid)/len(valid):.3f}")

valid range for pH: [0.0, 14.0]
  sample 3: 17.2 is OUTSIDE the physically possible pH range -- flagged, not averaged in
  sample 5: -0.4 is OUTSIDE the physically possible pH range -- flagged, not averaged in
valid readings kept = [6.8, 7.1, 6.9]
mean of valid readings only = 6.933
caveat: A value that PASSES the range check isn't automatically correct — range validation only catches impossible values, not plausible-but-wrong ones (e.g. a pH of 6.8 recorded for the wrong sample); it's a first filter, not a full audit.

title: Coercing/flagging non-numeric cells
definition: A column that's supposed to be all numbers sometimes contains a stray note ("N/A"), a unit accidentally typed into the cell ("12.9mA"), or a typo — and the question is what happens to that cell when the data gets imported. The dangerous failure mode is an importer that SILENTLY skips or drops any cell it can't parse as a number without telling you: your sample size quietly shrinks and nothing in the output flags that it happened, so the n you report in your writeup may not match what was actually analyzed.
whenToUse: Use this whenever you import spreadsheet or pasted data into any tool (including this game's own Data Terminal importer) — explicitly try to parse each cell as a number, and print/log every cell that fails, rather than trusting that a silent skip means “nothing to worry about.”
formula: numeric(x) = float(x) if parseable, else flag(x) and exclude

formulaBreakdown.meaning: the cell's text can be converted directly to a number with no leftover characters (a unit suffix like “mA” makes it NOT parseable).
log which cell failed and why, so the final analyzed n can be reconciled against the number of rows originally collected.

code:
import csv
import io

# Non-numeric cells (typed notes, "N/A", a stray unit suffix) in a numeric
# column -- must be explicitly coerced/flagged rather than silently dropped
# by whatever import path happens to choke on them (ties to how the Data
# Terminal's own CSV importer behaves: a row that fails to parse as a number
# is silently skipped, not counted as zero).
csv_text = """trial,current_ma
1,12.4
2,N/A
3,13.1
4,12.9mA
5,12.7"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
print("raw rows:")
for r in rows:
    print(f"  trial {r['trial']}: {r['current_ma']!r}")

numeric = []
flagged = []
for r in rows:
    raw = r["current_ma"]
    try:
        val = float(raw)
        numeric.append(val)
    except ValueError:
        flagged.append((r["trial"], raw))

print(f"cells that failed numeric coercion (flagged, not silently zeroed): {flagged}")
print(f"clean numeric values = {numeric}")
print(f"mean of clean values only = {sum(numeric)/len(numeric):.3f} mA (n={len(numeric)})")
print("caveat check: an importer that just skips non-numeric rows silently")
print("changes n without telling you -- always print/log how many rows were")
print("dropped so the sample size in your writeup matches what was analyzed.")

  trial 4: '12.9mA'

title: Handling censored / below-detection-limit values
definition: A censored (or "non-detect") reading is one where the instrument can only tell you the true value is BELOW some detection limit, not what it actually is — a water-quality sensor reporting "<0.5 ppb" for lead means the real concentration is somewhere between 0 and 0.5, not that it's exactly 0.5 or exactly 0. Substituting 0 for every censored value biases the mean downward (assumes the true value is at the very bottom of the possible range); substituting the detection limit itself biases it upward (assumes the worst case) — the common convention of substituting HALF the detection limit sits between those two biases as a reasonable compromise, though it's still a convention, not a real measurement.
whenToUse: Use this whenever a sensor or assay reports a “<limit” style non-detect rather than a numeric zero — explicitly choose and disclose a substitution convention (typically limit/2) rather than treating the censoring symbol as if it were data.
formula: substituted value = detection_limit / 2   (a convention, not a measurement)

formulaBreakdown.meaning: the smallest concentration/value the instrument can reliably distinguish from zero — anything below it reads as “<limit”, not a real number.
a widely used substitution that avoids the downward bias of using 0 and the upward bias of using the limit itself.

code:
import csv
import io

# Below-detection-limit (censored) values: a sensor reports "<0.5" rather
# than a real number. Substituting 0 biases the mean down; substituting the
# detection limit biases it up; the common convention is limit/2.
csv_text = """sample,lead_ppb
1,2.4
2,<0.5
3,3.1
4,<0.5
5,2.9"""

DETECTION_LIMIT = 0.5

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
print("raw rows:")
for r in rows:
    print(f"  sample {r['sample']}: {r['lead_ppb']!r}")

as_zero = []
as_limit = []
as_half_limit = []
for r in rows:
    raw = r["lead_ppb"]
    if raw.startswith("<"):
        as_zero.append(0.0)
        as_limit.append(DETECTION_LIMIT)
        as_half_limit.append(DETECTION_LIMIT / 2)
    else:
        v = float(raw)
        as_zero.append(v)
        as_limit.append(v)
        as_half_limit.append(v)

print(f"substitute 0 for censored:            {as_zero} -> mean = {sum(as_zero)/len(as_zero):.3f} ppb")
print(f"substitute detection limit itself:    {as_limit} -> mean = {sum(as_limit)/len(as_limit):.3f} ppb")
print(f"substitute limit/2 (the convention):  {as_half_limit} -> mean = {sum(as_half_limit)/len(as_half_limit):.3f} ppb")
print("caveat check: limit/2 sits between the biased-low (0) and biased-high")
print("(full limit) estimates -- it's a convention, not a measurement, so")
print("always report how censored values were handled alongside the result.")

title: Documenting every cleaning step
definition: Every decision made while cleaning a dataset — which rows were dropped, which values were flagged as sentinels, which duplicates were removed — needs to be written down as an explicit LOG, not just applied silently to produce a final “cleaned” file. Without that log, neither a reader nor your own future self can tell whether a reported sample size of n=4 means “4 trials were run” or “6 trials were run and 2 were quietly discarded” — and the two situations call for very different levels of trust in the result.
whenToUse: Use this as standard practice on every cleaning pass, no matter how small — keep a running log (even a simple list of “row X removed because Y”) alongside the cleaned dataset, and include a summary of it in your writeup's methods section.
formula: log = [ (row_id, reason_removed_or_changed) for every altered/dropped row ]

formulaBreakdown.meaning: which specific row/trial was affected — needed so the change can be traced back to the raw file.
WHY it was removed or changed — a sentinel code, a duplicate, a range violation — written down at cleaning time, not reconstructed from memory later.

code:
import csv
import io

# Documenting every cleaning step: a reproducible cleaning LOG (what was
# removed/changed and why) so the final n and mean can be traced back to the
# raw file -- not just a silently "cleaned" dataset with no paper trail.
csv_text = """trial,mass_g
1,10.2
2,10.5
3,-999
4,10.1
4,10.1
5,10.4"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
log = []
cleaned = []
seen_trials = set()

for r in rows:
    trial = r["trial"]
    raw = r["mass_g"]
    if raw == "-999":
        log.append(f"trial {trial}: removed -- sentinel value -999 means 'not measured'")
        continue
    if trial in seen_trials:
        log.append(f"trial {trial}: removed -- duplicate of an already-kept trial id")
        continue
    seen_trials.add(trial)
    cleaned.append(float(raw))

print("raw row count:", len(rows))
print("cleaning log:")
for entry in log:
    print(f"  - {entry}")
print(f"cleaned dataset (n={len(cleaned)}): {cleaned}")
print(f"mean = {sum(cleaned)/len(cleaned):.3f} g")
print("caveat check: without this log, a reader (or your future self) cannot")
print("tell whether n=4 means '4 trials were run' or '6 were run and 2 were")
print("quietly thrown away' -- always ship the log with the result.")

  - trial 4: removed -- duplicate of an already-kept trial id

title: Significant-figures counting rules
definition: Significant figures are the digits in a measurement that carry real information about its precision — counting them correctly requires a few specific rules: leading zeros (before the first nonzero digit) never count, because they only position the decimal point; a trailing zero AFTER a decimal point DOES count, because it was deliberately written to show precision; and trailing zeros in a whole number with NO decimal point are ambiguous — by convention they're not counted unless scientific notation removes the ambiguity. Getting this wrong means either overstating how precisely you actually measured something, or throwing away real precision your instrument gave you.
whenToUse: Use this the moment you read a number off any instrument or dataset and need to know how many of its digits you're actually entitled to trust and carry through a calculation.
formula: sig figs = digits from the first nonzero digit onward, following the leading/trailing-zero rules

formulaBreakdown.meaning: zeros before the first nonzero digit (like the two zeros in 0.0042) — never significant, they just place the decimal point.

formulaBreakdown.term: trailing zeros after a decimal point
formulaBreakdown.meaning: DO count (4.20 has 3 sig figs) — writing that zero is a deliberate claim of precision.
ambiguous (1200 could be 2, 3, or 4 sig figs) — by the convention used here, not counted unless removed via scientific notation.

code:
import csv
import io

csv_text = """reading,value
A,0.0042
B,4.20
C,1200
D,1.200e3"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))


def count_sig_figs(s: str) -> int:
    s = s.strip()
    if "e" in s.lower():
        mantissa = s.lower().split("e")[0]
        return count_sig_figs(mantissa)
    if "." in s:
        seen_nonzero = False
        sig = 0
        for ch in s:
            if ch == ".":
                continue
            if ch != "0":
                seen_nonzero = True
            if seen_nonzero:
                sig += 1
        return sig
    trimmed = s.rstrip("0")
    return len(trimmed) if trimmed else 1


for r in rows:
    n = count_sig_figs(r["value"])
    print(f"reading {r['reading']} = {r['value']!r} -> {n} significant figures")

print()
print("rules used above:")
print("  leading zeros (0.0042) never count -- only 4 and 2 are significant")
print("  a trailing zero AFTER a decimal point (4.20) DOES count")
print("  trailing zeros with NO decimal point (1200) are ambiguous -> not counted by default")
print("  writing the same value in scientific notation (1.200e3) removes the ambiguity -> 4 sig figs")
datasetNote: Four sample readings written in different formats, each testing a different sig-fig counting rule.
output:
reading A = '0.0042' -> 2 significant figures
reading B = '4.20' -> 3 significant figures
reading C = '1200' -> 2 significant figures
reading D = '1.200e3' -> 4 significant figures

  leading zeros (0.0042) never count -- only 4 and 2 are significant
  a trailing zero AFTER a decimal point (4.20) DOES count
  trailing zeros with NO decimal point (1200) are ambiguous -> not counted by default
  writing the same value in scientific notation (1.200e3) removes the ambiguity -> 4 sig figs
caveat: The “trailing zero with no decimal point” rule is a CONVENTION, not a law of physics — different textbooks disagree on it, which is exactly why switching to scientific notation is the recommended fix whenever it matters (see the trailing-zero-ambiguity entry).

title: Sig figs in addition/subtraction vs multiplication/division
definition: Addition and subtraction follow a DECIMAL PLACES rule: the result can only be trusted to as many decimal places as its LEAST precise input has — because you can't know a digit past where your least-precise measurement stops providing information. Multiplication and division instead follow a SIGNIFICANT FIGURES rule: the result can only be trusted to as many significant figures as the input with the FEWEST sig figs — a completely different rule from the addition case, and mixing the two up is one of the most common science-fair arithmetic mistakes.
whenToUse: Use the decimal-places rule immediately after any addition/subtraction step, and the fewest-sig-figs rule immediately after any multiplication/division step — in a multi-step calculation, apply the correct rule at EACH step, not just at the very end.
formula: add/sub: keep min(decimal places)   ·   mul/div: keep min(sig figs)

formulaBreakdown.meaning: count digits after the decimal point in each input; the result keeps only as many as the input with the FEWEST.
count total significant figures in each input; the result keeps only as many as the input with the FEWEST.

code:
import csv
import io

csv_text = """op,a,b
add,12.11,0.3
multiply,4.51,2.2"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))


def decimal_places(s: str) -> int:
    return len(s.split(".")[1]) if "." in s else 0


def sig_figs(s: str) -> int:
    s = s.lstrip("0").replace(".", "")
    return len(s) if s else 1


for r in rows:
    a_str, b_str = r["a"], r["b"]
    a, b = float(a_str), float(b_str)
    if r["op"] == "add":
        result = a + b
        dp_a, dp_b = decimal_places(a_str), decimal_places(b_str)
        keep_dp = min(dp_a, dp_b)
        rounded = round(result, keep_dp)
        print(f"ADD: {a_str} + {b_str} = {result} (raw)")
        print(f"  decimal places: {a_str} has {dp_a}, {b_str} has {dp_b}")
        print(f"  rule: keep only as many decimal places as the LEAST precise term ({keep_dp})")
        print(f"  rounded result = {rounded}")
    else:
        result = a * b
        sf_a, sf_b = sig_figs(a_str), sig_figs(b_str)
        keep_sf = min(sf_a, sf_b)
        # round to keep_sf significant figures
        from decimal import Decimal
        rounded = float(f"%.{keep_sf}g" % result)
        print(f"MULTIPLY: {a_str} x {b_str} = {result} (raw)")
        print(f"  sig figs: {a_str} has {sf_a}, {b_str} has {sf_b}")
        print(f"  rule: keep only as many sig figs as the term with the FEWEST sig figs ({keep_sf})")
        print(f"  rounded result = {rounded}")
datasetNote: Two small worked examples, one addition and one multiplication, each rounded by its own correct rule.
output:
ADD: 12.11 + 0.3 = 12.41 (raw)
  decimal places: 12.11 has 2, 0.3 has 1
  rule: keep only as many decimal places as the LEAST precise term (1)
  rounded result = 12.4
MULTIPLY: 4.51 x 2.2 = 9.922 (raw)
  sig figs: 4.51 has 3, 2.2 has 2
  rule: keep only as many sig figs as the term with the FEWEST sig figs (2)
  rounded result = 9.9
caveat: These two rules are NOT interchangeable — applying the sig-figs rule to an addition (or vice versa) gives a wrong answer even though both rules “feel” similar; always check which arithmetic operation you're rounding after.

title: Rounding rules (round-half-to-even)
definition: When the digit you're rounding away is EXACTLY 5 with nothing after it, naive “round half up” always rounds upward — but applied across a whole column of such cutoffs, that consistently nudges every result slightly higher, introducing a systematic bias. Round-half-to-even (“banker's rounding”) instead rounds to whichever neighboring digit is EVEN, so roughly half of all exact-.5 cases round up and half round down over a large dataset, cancelling the bias out — which is why it's the default behavior in Python's round(), IEEE 754 floating point, and most statistical software.
whenToUse: Use this (or at least know it's happening) whenever you round a long column of numbers that might land on exact half-way cutoffs — especially before comparing your own hand-rounded numbers against what a spreadsheet or programming language computed, since a mismatch is often just this rule.
formula: round(x) → nearest even digit when x lands exactly halfway between two round numbers

formulaBreakdown.meaning: the digit being dropped is precisely 5 with no further digits (2.5, 3.5, 0.125 at the relevant place) — the ONLY case this rule changes behavior for.
pick whichever of the two equally-close neighbors is an even digit, instead of always rounding up.

code:
import csv
import io

csv_text = """value,round_to_places
2.5,0
3.5,0
2.25,1
2.35,1
0.125,2"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))

for r in rows:
    v = float(r["value"])
    places = int(r["round_to_places"])
    naive_half_up = int(v * (10 ** places) + 0.5) / (10 ** places) if v >= 0 else v
    banker = round(v, places)  # Python's round() is round-half-to-even
    print(f"value={v}, round to {places} dp -> round-half-to-even (Python round()) = {banker}")

print()
print("round-half-to-even ('banker's rounding'): when the digit being dropped")
print("is EXACTLY 5 with nothing after it, round to whichever neighbor is")
print("EVEN, instead of always rounding up. This is why 2.5 -> 2 (2 is even)")
print("but 3.5 -> 4 (4 is even), not always 3 -> 3.")
print("Why it matters: naive round-half-up biases a long column of .5 cutoffs")
print("systematically upward; round-half-to-even cancels that bias out over")
print("many measurements, which is why it's the default in Python, IEEE 754,")
print("and most stats software.")

value=2.35, round to 1 dp -> round-half-to-even (Python round()) = 2.4

title: Dimensional analysis / unit-factor conversion
definition: Dimensional analysis converts a quantity from one unit to another by multiplying by a chain of conversion factors, each written as a fraction equal to 1 (like “1 km / 100,000 cm”), arranged so the unwanted units visibly CANCEL out step by step, leaving only the target unit. Writing out each factor explicitly (rather than just remembering “multiply by this number”) makes it obvious when a conversion is set up backwards, because the units simply won't cancel to the right thing if the fraction is inverted.
whenToUse: Use this any time a measured quantity needs to move between unit systems (cm/s to km/h, mL to L, grams to kilograms) — especially in a multi-step conversion where it's easy to lose track of whether you should multiply or divide by a factor.
formula: converted value = original value × (conversion factor 1) × (conversion factor 2) × …

formulaBreakdown.meaning: a fraction equal to exactly 1 (e.g. 1 km / 100000 cm) that lets you swap units without changing the actual quantity.
writing the factor with the unwanted unit on the opposite side from where it appears in the value lets it cancel algebraically, leaving the target unit.

code:
import csv
import io

# Dimensional analysis / unit-factor conversion: convert a measured speed
# from cm/s to km/h by chaining conversion factors so units visibly cancel.
csv_text = """quantity,value,unit
speed,850,cm/s"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
r = rows[0]
speed_cm_s = float(r["value"])

cm_to_km = 1 / 100_000  # 100,000 cm in 1 km
s_to_h = 3600  # 3600 s in 1 h

print(f"start: {speed_cm_s} cm/s")
print(f"conversion factors: 1 km = 100000 cm  ->  1 cm = {cm_to_km} km")
print(f"                     1 h = 3600 s")
step1 = speed_cm_s * cm_to_km
print(f"step 1 (cm -> km):  {speed_cm_s} cm/s * (1 km / 100000 cm) = {step1} km/s")
step2 = step1 * s_to_h
print(f"step 2 (s -> h):    {step1} km/s * (3600 s / 1 h) = {step2} km/h")
print(f"result: {speed_cm_s} cm/s = {step2:.1f} km/h")
datasetNote: A single speed measurement in cm/s, converted step by step into km/h via two chained conversion factors.
output:
start: 850.0 cm/s
conversion factors: 1 km = 100000 cm  ->  1 cm = 1e-05 km
                     1 h = 3600 s
step 1 (cm -> km):  850.0 cm/s * (1 km / 100000 cm) = 0.0085 km/s
step 2 (s -> h):    0.0085 km/s * (3600 s / 1 h) = 30.6 km/h
result: 850.0 cm/s = 30.6 km/h
caveat: If you set up a conversion factor upside down, the units won't cancel to what you want — always check that the unit you're trying to REMOVE appears in the denominator of the next factor, not the numerator.

title: SI prefixes
definition: SI prefixes (milli-, micro-, kilo-, etc.) attach a fixed power-of-ten multiplier to a base unit so very small or very large quantities can be written with manageable numbers instead of a long string of zeros — 3200 microamps is the same physical current as 0.0032 amps, just expressed with a different, more convenient prefix. Converting between a prefixed unit and its base unit (or between two different prefixes of the same base unit) is a special case of dimensional analysis: multiply by the prefix's known power-of-ten factor.
whenToUse: Use this whenever you need to combine or compare measurements that were recorded with different SI prefixes (e.g. one sensor logs in mV, another in V) — convert everything to the same base unit before doing any arithmetic between them.
formula: value in base unit = value × (prefix factor),  e.g. milli- = 10⁻³, micro- = 10⁻⁶, kilo- = 10³

formulaBreakdown.meaning: the fixed power of ten a given SI prefix represents (milli- = 0.001, micro- = 0.000001, kilo- = 1000, etc.).
the un-prefixed unit itself (grams, litres, amps) that every prefixed version is defined relative to.

code:
import csv
import io

csv_text = """quantity,value,unit
mass,2500,mg
volume,0.045,L
current,3200,uA"""

PREFIX_TO_BASE = {
    "u": 1e-6,
    "m": 1e-3,
    "": 1.0,
    "k": 1e3,
}

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
for r in rows:
    value = float(r["value"])
    unit = r["unit"]
    prefix = unit[0] if unit[0] in PREFIX_TO_BASE and len(unit) > 1 else ""
    base_unit = unit[len(prefix):]
    factor = PREFIX_TO_BASE[prefix]
    base_value = value * factor
    print(f"{value} {unit} : prefix '{prefix}' = x{factor:g} of the base unit '{base_unit}'")
    print(f"  -> {value} * {factor:g} = {base_value:g} {base_unit}")
datasetNote: Three measurements recorded with different SI prefixes (milligrams, litres with no prefix, and microamps).
output:
2500.0 mg : prefix 'm' = x0.001 of the base unit 'g'
  -> 2500.0 * 0.001 = 2.5 g
0.045 L : prefix '' = x1 of the base unit 'L'
  -> 0.045 * 1 = 0.045 L
3200.0 uA : prefix 'u' = x1e-06 of the base unit 'A'
  -> 3200.0 * 1e-06 = 0.0032 A
caveat: Mixing up milli- (10⁻³) and micro- (10⁻⁶) is a 1000x error that's easy to make when reading fast — always double check the prefix symbol (m vs μ/u) before converting, especially in handwritten lab notebooks where they can look similar.

title: Common science-fair unit traps
definition: A handful of unit mistakes show up again and again in science-fair projects: computing a RATIO or percentage change using Celsius (which has an arbitrary zero point, so “twice as hot” in °C is meaningless) instead of converting to the absolute Kelvin scale first; and conflating mass (grams, an amount of matter, unchanging anywhere) with weight (a FORCE in Newtons, caused by gravity, which changes depending on where you are). Milliliters and cubic centimeters, by contrast, really ARE numerically identical for water-like liquids — that one's not a trap, but it's easy to become suspicious of it once you've been burned by the other two.
whenToUse: Use this as a checklist right before computing any ratio, percentage, or physics formula involving temperature or mass — catch these two traps before they quietly produce a nonsense number that still looks plausible.
formula: ratio(T) must use Kelvin;  weight (N) = mass (kg) × g,  NOT weight = mass

formulaBreakdown.meaning: 0°C is the freezing point of water, not “zero heat” — so doubling a Celsius value does NOT mean doubling the actual thermal energy; only Kelvin (an absolute scale) supports that kind of ratio.
mass (g or kg) is an amount of matter and doesn't change; weight is the FORCE gravity exerts on that mass (in Newtons) and DOES change with location (e.g. the Moon).

code:
import csv
import io

csv_text = """label,value,unit
gas_temp_start,20,degC
gas_temp_end,40,degC
liquid_volume,50,mL
sample_mass,50,g"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
by_label = {r["label"]: (float(r["value"]), r["unit"]) for r in rows}

t1, _ = by_label["gas_temp_start"]
t2, _ = by_label["gas_temp_end"]

# TRAP 1: a ratio of temperatures must use an ABSOLUTE scale (Kelvin), not
# Celsius -- Celsius has an arbitrary zero point.
wrong_ratio = t2 / t1
t1_k, t2_k = t1 + 273.15, t2 + 273.15
correct_ratio = t2_k / t1_k
print("TRAP 1 -- ratio of temperatures must use an ABSOLUTE scale (Kelvin):")
print(f"  wrong (using degC directly): {t2}/{t1} = {wrong_ratio:.3f}x")
print(f"  correct (convert to Kelvin first): {t2_k:.2f}/{t1_k:.2f} = {correct_ratio:.3f}x")
print("  these disagree because 0 degC is NOT 'zero thermal energy' -- 0 K is.")

print()
vol_ml, _ = by_label["liquid_volume"]
mass_g, _ = by_label["sample_mass"]
g_earth = 9.81
weight_n = (mass_g / 1000) * g_earth
print("TRAP 2 -- mL and cm^3 ARE the same unit; mass (g) and weight (a force) are NOT:")
print(f"  {vol_ml:.0f} mL of water = {vol_ml:.0f} cm^3 of water (identical, for water at 4C)")
print(f"  a {mass_g:.0f} g mass has weight = mass(kg) * g = {mass_g/1000} kg * {g_earth} m/s^2 = {weight_n:.3f} N")
print(f"  the mass ({mass_g:.0f} g) stays the same on the Moon; the weight ({weight_n:.3f} N) does not.")

output:
TRAP 1 -- ratio of temperatures must use an ABSOLUTE scale (Kelvin):
  wrong (using degC directly): 40.0/20.0 = 2.000x
  correct (convert to Kelvin first): 313.15/293.15 = 1.068x
  these disagree because 0 degC is NOT 'zero thermal energy' -- 0 K is.

TRAP 2 -- mL and cm^3 ARE the same unit; mass (g) and weight (a force) are NOT:
  50 mL of water = 50 cm^3 of water (identical, for water at 4C)
  a 50 g mass has weight = mass(kg) * g = 0.05 kg * 9.81 m/s^2 = 0.491 N
  the mass (50 g) stays the same on the Moon; the weight (0.491 N) does not.
caveat: Both traps produce an answer that LOOKS reasonable at a glance — “twice as hot” and “50 g weighs 50 N” both sound plausible until you check the actual physics, which is exactly what makes them dangerous rather than obviously wrong.

title: Precision vs accuracy
definition: Precision describes how tightly repeated measurements of the SAME thing cluster together (a small SD means high precision), while accuracy describes how close the measurements' average sits to the TRUE, correct value (a small bias means high accuracy) — and critically, these are independent of each other. An instrument can be highly precise (very reproducible, tiny SD) while still being systematically wrong (biased away from the true value) if it's miscalibrated; that combination — precise but inaccurate — is exactly the failure mode a calibration check (see Measurement & uncertainty) is designed to catch.
whenToUse: Use these as two SEPARATE checks on any instrument or method: compute the SD across repeats for precision, and compare the mean against a known true/reference value for accuracy — never assume one implies the other.
formula: precision = SD of repeated readings;   accuracy = |mean − true value| (bias)

formulaBreakdown.meaning: how spread out repeated readings of the SAME quantity are — small SD = tightly clustered = precise.
how far the AVERAGE of those readings sits from the actual, known-correct value — small bias = accurate.

datasetCsv:
instrument,trial,reading_g
scale_A,1,50.1
scale_A,2,50.2
scale_A,3,50.0
scale_A,4,50.1
scale_B,1,52.4
scale_B,2,48.1
scale_B,3,51.0
scale_B,4,49.3
code:
import csv
import io

# Precision vs accuracy: precision = how tightly repeated readings cluster
# (SD); accuracy = how close the mean sits to the TRUE/known value. A
# miscalibrated instrument can be highly precise but inaccurate.
csv_text = """instrument,trial,reading_g
scale_A,1,50.1
scale_A,2,50.2
scale_A,3,50.0
scale_A,4,50.1
scale_B,1,52.4
scale_B,2,48.1
scale_B,3,51.0
scale_B,4,49.3"""

TRUE_MASS = 50.0

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
for name in ["scale_A", "scale_B"]:
    readings = [float(r["reading_g"]) for r in rows if r["instrument"] == name]
    n = len(readings)
    mean = sum(readings) / n
    sd = (sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in readings) / (n - 1)) ** 0.5
    bias = mean - TRUE_MASS
    print(f"{name}: readings = {readings}")
    print(f"  mean = {mean:.2f} g, SD (precision) = {sd:.3f} g, bias vs true {TRUE_MASS}g (accuracy) = {bias:+.2f} g")

print()
print("scale_A is PRECISE (small SD, tightly clustered) AND ACCURATE (mean close to true 50.0 g).")
print("scale_B is IMPRECISE (large SD, scattered) but happens to be roughly ACCURATE on average.")
print("a scale could also be precise-but-inaccurate: tightly clustered around the WRONG value -- that's what a calibration check catches.")
datasetNote: Four repeated readings each from two different scales weighing the same known 50.0 g reference mass.
output:
scale_A: readings = [50.1, 50.2, 50.0, 50.1]
  mean = 50.10 g, SD (precision) = 0.082 g, bias vs true 50.0g (accuracy) = +0.10 g
scale_B: readings = [52.4, 48.1, 51.0, 49.3]
  mean = 50.20 g, SD (precision) = 1.889 g, bias vs true 50.0g (accuracy) = +0.20 g

scale_A is PRECISE (small SD, tightly clustered) AND ACCURATE (mean close to true 50.0 g).
scale_B is IMPRECISE (large SD, scattered) but happens to be roughly ACCURATE on average.
a scale could also be precise-but-inaccurate: tightly clustered around the WRONG value -- that's what a calibration check catches.
caveat: A scale can be PRECISE but INACCURATE (tightly clustered around the wrong number) — a small SD alone is never enough evidence that an instrument is trustworthy; you also need a known reference value to check the mean against.

title: Trailing-zero ambiguity and scientific notation as the fix
definition: A whole number ending in zeros, like 1500, is genuinely ambiguous about how many of those digits are significant — it could mean a rough measurement good to only 2 sig figs (1.5 × 10³), or a precise one good to 4 (1.500 × 10³), and the plain digit string “1500” cannot tell a reader which was intended. Scientific notation resolves this completely by only ever writing the digits that are actually significant in the mantissa, so “1.5e3” and “1.500e3” are unambiguous about precision in a way “1500” never can be.
whenToUse: Use scientific notation any time a whole-number measurement ends in one or more zeros AND you need the reader to know exactly how many of those digits are significant — which is most of the time in a formal science-fair writeup.
formula: N.NNN × 10ᵉ  (only significant digits appear in the mantissa)

formulaBreakdown.meaning: the digit string before the × 10ᵉ — every digit written there IS significant, with no ambiguity.
the power of ten that repositions the decimal point — it carries no precision information of its own.

code:
import csv
import io

# Trailing-zero ambiguity: "1500 m" could mean 2, 3, or 4 sig figs depending
# on what the recorder intended -- scientific notation removes the ambiguity
# by only ever writing the digits that are actually significant.
csv_text = """reading,value_m,intended_sig_figs
distance,1500,2
distance_precise,1500,4"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))

for r in rows:
    value = float(r["value_m"])
    sig = int(r["intended_sig_figs"])
    # write in scientific notation with (sig - 1) digits after the decimal
    mantissa_digits = sig - 1
    exponent = 3  # 1500 = 1.5 x 10^3
    mantissa = value / (10 ** exponent)
    sci = f"{mantissa:.{mantissa_digits}f}e{exponent}"
    print(f"'{value:.0f} m' meant to have {sig} sig figs -> ambiguous as written")
    print(f"  scientific notation removes the ambiguity: {sci} m ({sig} sig figs, unambiguous)")

print()
print("the plain digit string '1500' cannot distinguish '1.5 x 10^3' (2 sig")
print("figs, a rough estimate) from '1.500 x 10^3' (4 sig figs, a precise")
print("measurement) -- always switch to scientific notation whenever trailing")
print("zeros in a whole number could be misread as precision you don't have.")
datasetNote: The same plain digit string, 1500, intended to represent two different precisions — shown resolved via scientific notation.
output:
'1500 m' meant to have 2 sig figs -> ambiguous as written
  scientific notation removes the ambiguity: 1.5e3 m (2 sig figs, unambiguous)
'1500 m' meant to have 4 sig figs -> ambiguous as written
  scientific notation removes the ambiguity: 1.500e3 m (4 sig figs, unambiguous)

the plain digit string '1500' cannot distinguish '1.5 x 10^3' (2 sig
figs, a rough estimate) from '1.500 x 10^3' (4 sig figs, a precise
measurement) -- always switch to scientific notation whenever trailing
zeros in a whole number could be misread as precision you don't have.
caveat: Once a number is already written in scientific notation, EVERY digit in the mantissa counts as significant, including trailing zeros — don't apply the “plain-number” trailing-zero-is-ambiguous rule to a value that's already in scientific form.

title: Unit consistency check before computing a derived quantity
definition: Before combining two or more measured quantities into a derived one (like dividing a distance by a time to get a speed), every input needs to be in a mutually CONSISTENT unit system — dividing kilometers by seconds silently produces a number in km/s, technically “correct” arithmetic but almost certainly not the unit you meant to report or compare against anything else. The fix is a deliberate pre-calculation step: convert every input to the same base-unit system FIRST, then compute the derived quantity, then convert the result to whatever human-friendly unit you actually want to present.
whenToUse: Use this as a mandatory checkpoint immediately before any formula that combines two or more measured quantities — write down each input's unit explicitly and convert to a common system before touching a calculator.
formula: check: are all inputs in the SAME base-unit system? if not — convert first, THEN compute.

formulaBreakdown.meaning: a single consistent set of units (e.g. all SI base units: meters, seconds, kilograms) that every input gets converted into before combining.
the unit conversion happens BEFORE the arithmetic, not as an afterthought applied to a wrong-unit answer.

import csv
import io

# Unit-consistency check before computing a derived quantity: speed = distance/time
# -- mixing km (distance) with seconds (time) silently gives a nonsense number
# unless every input is converted to a common, consistent unit system first.
csv_text = """quantity,value,unit
distance,2.5,km
time,45,s"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
by_q = {r["quantity"]: (float(r["value"]), r["unit"]) for r in rows}

dist_val, dist_unit = by_q["distance"]
time_val, time_unit = by_q["time"]

wrong_speed = dist_val / time_val
print(f"WRONG (units not checked first): {dist_val} {dist_unit} / {time_val} {time_unit} = {wrong_speed:.4f} (km/s?? -- but is that really what we measured?)")

# Consistency check: convert distance to meters (SI base) before dividing by
# time already in seconds (SI base).
dist_m = dist_val * 1000
print(f"consistency check: convert distance to the SAME base-unit system as time first")
print(f"  {dist_val} km * 1000 = {dist_m:.0f} m   (time is already in s)")
correct_speed = dist_m / time_val
print(f"correct: {dist_m:.0f} m / {time_val} s = {correct_speed:.3f} m/s")
print(f"convert back for a human-friendly unit if needed: {correct_speed*3.6:.2f} km/h")

  2.5 km * 1000 = 2500 m   (time is already in s)
correct: 2500 m / 45.0 s = 55.556 m/s

caveat: A calculator will happily compute distance/time even when the units are inconsistent — it has no way to warn you the result is in a nonsensical mixed unit; that check has to come from you, before the division, not after.

title: Outlier-removal policy — legitimate exclusion vs p-hacking
definition: Deciding whether to exclude an outlier from your analysis is an ETHICS and POLICY question, not a computational one — the arithmetic for detecting a statistical outlier (the 1.5×IQR fence) is covered in the Stats Guide's IQR & outlier detection entry and is not repeated here. What matters is WHY a point is excluded: a legitimate exclusion has a reason tied to the MEASUREMENT PROCESS, documented at the time it happened (a probe slipping, a contaminated sample, a logged instrument fault) — independent of whether that point helps or hurts your hypothesis. P-hacking is the mirror image: noticing, after the fact, that removing an inconvenient point moves your result in the direction you wanted, and only THEN inventing a justification for excluding it.
whenToUse: Use this any time a data point looks unusual and you're tempted to drop it — ask whether you can point to a documented, outcome-independent reason for the exclusion; if the only reason is “it made my result look better/worse,” it must stay in.
formula: legitimate: reason documented BEFORE outcome is known.   p-hacking: reason invented AFTER seeing the outcome.

formulaBreakdown.meaning: the reason for a possible exclusion (a lab-notebook note about a probe slipping) exists independent of, and before, seeing whether it changes the result.
the justification for exclusion has nothing to do with which DIRECTION it pushes the mean/p-value — that's the line between a legitimate call and p-hacking.

title: Pre-declaring exclusion criteria
definition: The strongest defense against outlier-removal turning into p-hacking is to write down the EXACT rule for what counts as excludable before you've even looked at how the data came out — e.g. “any trial where the thermometer fault light was logged gets excluded,” decided and written down before running trial 1. Applying that rule afterward is then purely mechanical: the same rule, applied to the same data, gives the same exclusions no matter who checks it or what answer they were hoping for — which is exactly what makes a post-hoc decision (“this one also looks too high, let's drop it too”) indistinguishable from cherry-picking.
whenToUse: Use this at the start of an experiment, before data collection begins — write your exclusion criteria into your lab notebook or protocol FIRST, then apply them mechanically regardless of how the numbers turn out.
formula: predeclared rule (fixed in advance) applied mechanically to every trial, regardless of outcome

formulaBreakdown.meaning: written down and fixed BEFORE the data exists — can't be adjusted after seeing which points are inconvenient.
the same rule is checked against every trial the same way — no judgment calls made once results are visible.

import csv
import io

# Pre-declaring exclusion criteria: write the rule for what counts as
# excludable BEFORE collecting/looking at the data, then apply it mechanically.
# Contrast with choosing criteria AFTER seeing the data (which can be steered
# to whatever answer you want -- same numbers, different p(bias)).
csv_text = """trial,germination_time_hr,thermometer_fault_logged
1,18.2,no
2,19.1,no
3,45.0,yes
4,18.9,no
5,17.8,no
6,52.0,no"""

# Pre-declared rule (written down BEFORE this trial ran): "exclude a reading
# only if the thermometer fault was logged during that trial."
PREDECLARED_RULE = "thermometer_fault_logged == 'yes'"

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
print(f"pre-declared rule (written down before data collection): {PREDECLARED_RULE}")

kept_predeclared = [r for r in rows if r["thermometer_fault_logged"] == "no"]
excluded_predeclared = [r for r in rows if r["thermometer_fault_logged"] == "yes"]
print(f"excluded by the pre-declared rule: trial {[r['trial'] for r in excluded_predeclared]}")

vals_predeclared = [float(r["germination_time_hr"]) for r in kept_predeclared]
mean_predeclared = sum(vals_predeclared) / len(vals_predeclared)
print(f"mean under the pre-declared rule = {mean_predeclared:.2f} hr (n={len(vals_predeclared)})")

print()
# Post-hoc alternative: someone instead decides, AFTER seeing all 6 numbers,
# to also drop trial 6 (52.0) because "it looks too high" -- no rule for it
# existed beforehand, it's simply the next most inconvenient number.
posthoc_kept = [r for r in rows if r["trial"] not in ("3", "6")]
vals_posthoc = [float(r["germination_time_hr"]) for r in posthoc_kept]
mean_posthoc = sum(vals_posthoc) / len(vals_posthoc)
print("post-hoc alternative: also drop trial 6 (52.0) because it 'looks too")
print("high', even though no fault was logged and no rule for it existed")
print("before the data came in:")
print(f"mean if trial 6 is ALSO dropped post-hoc = {mean_posthoc:.2f} hr (n={len(vals_posthoc)})")
print("the pre-declared rule is defensible because it can't be bent by the")
print("result; the post-hoc drop can't be distinguished from cherry-picking.")
